papers.title: Local ROS and inefficient autophagosome formation limit Optineurin-mediated mitophagy in neurons
papers.summary: This paper investigates why neurons struggle to clear damaged mitochondria using Optineurin-mediated mitophagy. The researchers find that localized reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and poor formation of autophagosomes (the vesicles that engulf damaged mitochondria) are key bottlenecks in this process. This suggests neurons have specific vulnerabilities in mitochondrial quality control compared to other cell types.
papers.why: This directly addresses core mechanisms of neuronal mitophagy and autophagosome dynamics, which are central to understanding mitochondrial quality control in brain cells relevant to the PhD project.

papers.title: ST-DISTAL: Dual-Branch Graph Convolution with Distributional Alignment for Cell-Type Deconvolution
papers.summary: ST-DISTAL is a new computational method for figuring out what mix of cell types is present in each spot of spatial transcriptomics data, a problem called cell-type deconvolution. It uses a dual-branch graph convolutional neural network combined with a distributional alignment technique to improve accuracy. The approach likely helps researchers more precisely map where specific cell types sit within tissue sections.
papers.why: Accurate deconvolution tools like this could help resolve interneuron subtypes and their spatial relationship to perineuronal nets in spatial transcriptomics datasets from brain tissue.

papers.title: Minding the gates: dual cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous mechanisms of TBK1 in ALS/FTD
papers.summary: This paper discusses TBK1, a gene linked to ALS/FTD, and how it acts through both cell-autonomous (within the affected neuron itself) and non-cell-autonomous (via surrounding cells like glia) mechanisms. TBK1 is known to regulate autophagy and mitophagy, as well as innate immune signaling, and its dysfunction contributes to neurodegeneration through multiple cellular pathways. The abstract appears to be a review or commentary synthesizing how TBK1's dual roles 'mind the gates' between neurons and their environment in disease progression.
papers.why: TBK1 is a key regulator of mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, directly relevant to the mechanistic focus of this PhD project even though it centers on ALS/FTD rather than the specific interneuron/PNN context.

papers.title: Applications of single-cell transcriptomics in glaucoma research: from the aqueous humor outflow pathway to retinal ganglion cell neurodegeneration
papers.summary: This paper reviews how single-cell transcriptomics has been used to study glaucoma, a disease involving damage to retinal ganglion cells and their axons. It covers insights into the aqueous humor outflow pathway, which regulates eye pressure, and how single-cell approaches reveal mechanisms of retinal ganglion cell neurodegeneration. The review likely summarizes cell-type-specific gene expression changes and potential therapeutic targets identified through these technologies.
papers.why: While focused on glaucoma and the eye rather than brain interneurons, this review offers transferable insights into single-cell transcriptomic approaches for studying neurodegeneration that could inform analysis strategies for neuronal vulnerability and spatial transcriptomics workflows in the PhD project.

papers.title: Expression and role of HSPA5 in environmental toxin-induced neurological disorders
papers.summary: This paper discusses HSPA5 (also known as BiP/GRP78), a key endoplasmic reticulum chaperone protein, and its involvement in neurological disorders caused by environmental toxins. It likely reviews how toxin exposure triggers ER stress responses mediated by HSPA5, contributing to neuronal dysfunction or damage. The abstract suggests a focus on molecular mechanisms linking environmental toxicants to neurodegeneration through this stress-response pathway.
papers.why: ER stress and chaperone-mediated proteostasis pathways like HSPA5 intersect with autophagy and mitophagy regulation in neurons, making this relevant background for understanding toxin-induced neuronal stress responses that may trigger protective or pathological clearance mechanisms.

papers.title: Host miRNA orchestration of mitophagy pathways during bacterial infection: current advances and future directions
papers.summary: This paper reviews how host microRNAs regulate mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria, during bacterial infections. It discusses the molecular pathways through which miRNAs influence mitochondrial quality control as part of the innate immune response. The review also outlines current knowledge gaps and future research directions in this field.
papers.why: While focused on infection biology rather than neurons, the paper's deep dive into miRNA regulation of mitophagy pathways could offer mechanistic insights transferable to understanding neuronal mitophagy regulation relevant to your project.
